rationale: A wins because it has discipline: three real angles, no padded trophy shelf, and it refuses the tempting junk before it contaminates the pitch. A's strongest line, "Replit's Agent Promises Working Apps. It Won't Say How Often They Actually Work," turns the missing reliability data into a clean reporter question. B has useful material, but "When the software writes itself, you pay by the job — not by the seat" builds a business-model thesis the facts do not support. That is how a decent angle set wanders into deckware.
gaps_in_A: "Replit contradicting its own founding premise" overstates the education fact. The update says Replit is used heavily in education, not that teaching coding was its founding premise.

"the market has moved from AI that assists developers to AI that replaces the development workflow" is too broad for a single company launch. A correctly asks for comparable offerings, but the angle headline still gets ahead of the proof.
"explicitly declines to disclose reliability rates" is sharper than the supplied fact. The update says reliability is not disclosed; it does not say Replit was asked and declined.
gaps_in_B: "you pay by the job — not by the seat" invents the unit of pricing. The update only says usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions; it does not establish per-job pricing or a per-seat-to-consumption shift.
"writes the code for students" assumes student access and classroom use of the agent. The update says Replit is used heavily in education, not that this agent is available to students.
"CS teachers are already arguing about" and "this school year" add a convenient education peg without supplied evidence. Nice calendar seasoning, still seasoning.
"No current news signal was supplied" is wrong. The launch is the current news signal, and sending the founder to `newsjack-detector` before closing proof gaps is busywork with a hat on.
